title: Transparency and translucency
wiki_lead:
In the field of optics, transparency (also called pellucidity or diaphaneity) is the physical property of allowing light to pass through the material without appreciable scattering of light. On a macroscopic scale (one in which the dimensions are much larger than the wavelengths of the photons in question), the photons can be said to follow Snell's law. Translucency (also called translucence or translucidity) is the physical property of allowing light to pass through the material (with or without scattering of light). It allows light to pass through but the light does not necessarily follow Snell's law on the macroscopic scale; the photons may be scattered at either of the two interfaces, or internally, where there is a change in the index of refraction. In other words, a translucent material is made up of components with different indices of refraction, while a transparent material is made up of components with a uniform index of refraction. Transparent materials appear clear, with the overall appearance of one color, or any combination leading up to a brilliant spectrum of every color. The opposite property of translucency is opacity. Other categories of visual appearance, related to the perception of regular or diffuse reflection and transmission of light, have been organized under the concept of cesia in an order system with three variables, including transparency, translucency and opacity among the involved aspects.
When light encounters a material, it can interact with it in several different ways. These interactions depend on the wavelength of the light and the nature of the material. Photons interact with an object by some combination of reflection, absorption and transmission.
Some materials, such as plate glass and clean water, transmit much of the light that falls on them and reflect little of it; such materials are called optically transparent. Many liquids and aqueous solutions are highly transparent. Absence of structural defects (voids, cracks, etc.) and molecular structure of most liquids are mostly responsible for excellent optical transmission.
Materials that do not transmit light are called opaque. Many such substances have a chemical composition which includes what are referred to as absorption centers. Many substances are selective in their absorption of white light frequencies. They absorb certain portions of the visible spectrum while reflecting others. The frequencies of the spectrum which are not absorbed are either reflected or transmitted for our physical observation. This is what gives rise to color. The attenuation of light of all frequencies and wavelengths is due to the combined mechanisms of absorption and scattering.
Transparency can provide almost perfect camouflage for animals  able to achieve it. This is easier in dimly-lit or turbid seawater than in good illumination. Many marine animals such as jellyfish are highly transparent.

Etymology
late Middle English: from Old French, from medieval Latin transparent- 'visible through', from Latin transparere, from trans- 'through' + parere 'be visible'.
late 16th century (in the Latin sense): from Latin translucent- 'shining through', from the verb translucere, from trans- 'through' + lucere 'to shine'.
late Middle English opake, from Latin opacus 'darkened'. The current spelling (rare before the 19th century) has been influenced by the French form.

grok_lead: Transparency and translucency are fundamental optical properties of materials that govern the transmission of visible light through them, distinguishing how clearly or diffusely objects behind the material can be perceived. In physics, transparency occurs when a material permits light to pass through with minimal scattering or absorption, allowing undistorted images of objects on the opposite side to be visible, as quantified by a transmittance (Ï) approaching 1, where absorptance (a) and reflectance (Ï) are near 0. Examples include clear glass or pure water, where light travels in straight paths due to low interaction with the material's atomic structure. Conversely, translucency involves partial transmission of light accompanied by significant subsurface scattering, which diffuses the light and blurs the view of transmitted objects, with 0 < Ï < 1 and combined a + Ï < 1. Common translucent materials, such as frosted glass, milk, or human skin, exhibit this property because light penetrates the surface, scatters internally via mechanisms like Rayleigh or Mie scattering, and re-emerges, creating a softened glow without sharp details. These properties arise from the fundamental interactions of light with matter, governed by the material's refractive index, absorption coefficient (Î±), and scattering events, as described by the Beer-Lambert law for attenuation: Ï = exp(-Î±t), where t is thickness. In transparent materials, the mean free path of photons is much longer than the material's dimensions, minimizing diffusion, whereas in translucent ones, frequent scattering eventsâoften quantified by scattering coefficientsâlead to multiple internal reflections and a hazy appearance. Opacity, the opposite extreme (Ï = 0), results when light is fully absorbed or reflected, as in metals or dense pigments, completing the spectrum from full penetration to blockage. Standards from organizations like the International Commission on Illumination (CIE) define transparency as transmission without diffusion, while the American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM) emphasizes diffuse transmission in translucency, aiding precise measurement via haze or clarity indices. Beyond physics, transparency and translucency have perceptual dimensions, as the human visual system interprets these cues through luminance gradients, edge sharpness, and contrast reduction to infer material qualities. For instance, backlighting enhances the perception of translucency by highlighting subsurface light transport, influencing judgments in fields like materials science, where translucent polymers are engineered for displays, or biology, where skin's translucency affects appearance. These properties are crucial in optics applications, from optical fibers relying on transparency to diffusers exploiting translucency, and continue to be studied for advanced rendering in computer graphics and biomedical imaging.
